question: What are HTTP status code ranges and what does each range mean?
title: HTTP Status Code Ranges
direct_answer: HTTP status codes are grouped in ranges: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirects, 4xx client errors, 5xx server errors. In REST APIs, the most important are 2xx (success) and 4xx/5xx (errors).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know standard HTTP status codes and use them correctly
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning 200 for everything and putting error info in the response body
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show you know the nuanced codes like 201, 204, 409, 422

sections.title: Status Code Semantics
sections.content: HTTP status codes communicate the outcome of a request in a standardized way. Using them correctly means API consumers (mobile apps, frontend, other services) can handle responses programmatically without parsing error messages.

sections.title: Key Status Codes by Range
content: 2xx Success: 200 OK, 201 Created (POST), 204 No Content (DELETE)
3xx Redirect: 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified (cache hit)
4xx Client Error: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden (not authorized), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable Entity (validation)
5xx Server Error: 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: HTTP status codes fall into five ranges. 2xx means success — 200 for GET reads, 201 for POST creates, 204 when DELETE succeeds with no body. 3xx are redirects. 4xx are client errors — the client did something wrong. 5xx are server errors — something went wrong on our side. A common mistake I've seen is returning 200 for everything and putting 'error: true' in the JSON body — that breaks clients that rely on the status code to detect errors. Using the right status codes is important for API consumers.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Status codes are how the server tells the client what happened — learn the ranges and the key codes in each one.

beats.text: HTTP status codes communicate the outcome of a request in a standardized, machine-readable way. They are grouped into five ranges by the hundreds digit. Clients — mobile apps, browsers, other services — use the code to decide what to do next without parsing the response body.

If every API invented its own way to signal errors in the body, every client would need custom logic. Status codes give a universal language: 200 means success everywhere, 404 means not found everywhere, 500 means server problem everywhere.

items: 2xx success: 200 OK (GET/PUT), 201 Created (POST), 204 No Content (DELETE)
3xx redirect: 301 Moved Permanently, 304 Not Modified (cache hit)
4xx client error: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthenticated, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Validation
5xx server error: 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable

beats.text: Todo app responses: GET /todos returns 200 with the list. POST /todos returns 201 with the created todo. DELETE /todos/42 returns 204 with no body. GET /todos/999 where 999 doesn't exist returns 404. POST /todos with an invalid body returns 400 or 422. An unhandled exception in the server returns 500. In Spring Boot, ResponseEntity.ok(), ResponseEntity.created(), ResponseEntity.noContent(), ResponseEntity.notFound() map directly to these codes. candidates miss: many candidates return 200 for everything and put error: true in the body. That breaks any client that relies on the status code — which is all of them.

items: Returning 200 for error cases with error info in the body — HTTP clients check the status code; a 200 looks like success
Using only 200 and 500 — the nuanced codes like 201, 204, 404, 409, 422 communicate intent that 200 cannot

speakable_v2.cap: 2xx = success. 4xx = client did something wrong. 5xx = server problem. Within 2xx: 200 for reads, 201 for creates, 204 for deletes. Know these and you're ahead of most freshers.

question: What is the difference between 401 Unauthorized and 403 Forbidden?
title: 401 vs 403 Status Codes
direct_answer: 401 Unauthorized means authentication failed or is missing — the client is not logged in. 403 Forbidden means authentication succeeded but authorization failed — the user is logged in but doesn't have permission.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise understanding of authentication vs authorization, mapped to status codes
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing the two or using 403 when 401 is correct
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect 401 to WWW-Authenticate header and Spring Security's behavior

sections.title: Authentication vs Authorization in Status Codes
sections.content: Despite its name, 401 Unauthorized really means 'unauthenticated' — you need to log in first. 403 Forbidden means 'unauthorized' — you're logged in, but this resource isn't for you. The naming is historically confusing but the distinction is critical for security.

sections.title: When to Return Each
content: 401: No token, expired token, invalid token — authenticate first
403: Valid token, but role/permission insufficient — you're logged in, but no access
Spring Security: UsernameNotFoundException or BadCredentialsException → 401
Spring Security: AccessDeniedException → 403
401 response should include WWW-Authenticate header per HTTP spec
Security tip: some APIs return 404 instead of 403 to not reveal resource existence

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The names are confusing but the distinction is important. 401 means you're not authenticated — you haven't proved who you are yet, usually because the JWT is missing or expired. 403 means you are authenticated — the server knows who you are — but you're not allowed to do this action. For example, a regular user trying to access an admin endpoint gets 403. In Spring Security, these map to different exceptions: 401 for authentication failures and 403 for access denial.

groups.label: 401 Unauthorized
groups.text: The client has not authenticated. No token, expired token, or invalid token. Despite the name 'Unauthorized', 401 really means unauthenticated — identity is not established.

groups.label: 403 Forbidden
groups.text: The client is authenticated — the server knows who they are — but they lack permission for this resource. It's an authorization failure, not an identity failure.

rows.axis: Valid JWT, USER role, endpoint needs ADMIN

items: Return 401 when the request has no valid credentials — the client should authenticate and retry
Return 403 when credentials are valid but access is denied — the client should not retry without a role change

beats.text: Todo app: unauthenticated GET /todos returns 401 (no JWT). Authenticated GET /admin/stats with USER role returns 403. In Spring Security, AuthenticationException maps to 401 and AccessDeniedException maps to 403. The ExceptionTranslationFilter handles this automatically. sharp edge: the HTTP spec named 401 'Unauthorized' but it really means unauthenticated. This trips up nearly everyone the first time. Memorize it: 401 = unauthenticated, 403 = unauthorized.

speakable_v2.cap: 401 = not authenticated (prove who you are). 403 = authenticated but not allowed. Spring Security maps authentication failures to 401 and access denial to 403 automatically.

question: When do you return 200 OK vs 201 Created vs 204 No Content?
title: 200 vs 201 vs 204 Status Codes
direct_answer: Return 200 OK for successful GET, PUT, PATCH responses with a body. Return 201 Created after a successful POST that creates a resource — include a Location header. Return 204 No Content for successful DELETE with no response body.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise status code usage showing REST best practices
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning 200 for POST creates — missing the 201 with Location header
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Location header for 201 and using ResponseEntity in Spring Boot

sections.title: Success Status Code Selection
sections.content: Within the 2xx range, choosing the right code communicates exactly what happened. Many developers default to 200 for everything, but 201 and 204 carry additional semantic meaning that clients can use — 201 tells the client where the new resource lives, 204 tells it not to wait for a body.

sections.title: Usage Rules
content: 200 OK: GET with body, PUT/PATCH with updated resource in body
201 Created: POST that creates resource — add Location: /users/123 header
204 No Content: DELETE success, PUT/PATCH when you don't return body
202 Accepted: async operation started, result not ready yet
In Spring Boot: return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create('/users/' + id)).body(user)
204 means no response body — client must not expect one

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: For successful responses, I use 200 for GETs and updates that return the modified resource, 201 after POST creates — and I add a Location header pointing to the new resource URL, which is per the HTTP spec. For DELETE, I return 204 No Content since there's nothing to return. In Spring Boot, the cleanest way is ResponseEntity.created() which sets both the 201 status and the Location header. These nuances matter in professional codebases because client SDKs rely on the status code to know what to expect in the body.

followup_questions: What should the Location header contain after a 201?

seo.metaTitle: 200 vs 201 vs 204 HTTP Status Codes | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn when to use 200 201 204 HTTP status codes in REST APIs. Spring Boot Java fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Within the 2xx range, the specific code tells clients whether to expect a body and where to find the new resource.

beats.text: Choosing among 200, 201, and 204 is about giving clients precise information: did something get created, did you get content back, or was this a silent success?

items: 200 OK: success with a response body — use for GET reads and PUT/PATCH when returning the updated resource
201 Created: a new resource was created — use for POST; include a Location header pointing to the new resource URI
204 No Content: success with no body — use for DELETE, and for PUT/PATCH when you don't return the resource

beats.text: Rule of thumb: if your endpoint creates something, return 201 and set the Location header. If it deletes or updates silently, return 204. For everything else that succeeds with a body, return 200.

items: You're returning 200 for a POST create — 201 signals creation and gives the client the new resource URI in Location
You're returning 200 for DELETE — 204 is correct; a DELETE response body is not expected

speakable_v2.cap: 200 = success with body. 201 = created (add Location header). 204 = success, no body. Three rules, nearly every success response covered.

question: When do you use 400 Bad Request vs 404 Not Found vs 409 Conflict vs 422 Unprocessable Entity?
title: 4xx Status Code Distinctions
direct_answer: 400 for malformed request syntax. 404 when resource doesn't exist. 409 for state conflicts (duplicate entry). 422 for syntactically correct but semantically invalid requests (validation failures).

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise error handling knowledge and API design maturity
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using 400 for everything or confusing 409 and 422
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show you know that Spring Boot @Valid returns 400 but 422 is more semantically correct for validation

sections.title: 4xx Error Code Selection
sections.content: The 4xx range indicates client-side errors, but the specific code tells the client how to respond. 400 says 'fix your request format', 404 says 'this doesn't exist', 409 says 'there's a conflict with current state', 422 says 'the data is valid JSON but the values are wrong'.

sections.title: When to Use Each
content: 400 Bad Request: Malformed JSON, missing required fields, wrong data type
404 Not Found: Resource with that ID doesn't exist
409 Conflict: Username already taken, duplicate email, version conflict (optimistic locking)
422 Unprocessable Entity: Validation failures (age < 0, email format wrong, future date required)
410 Gone: Resource permanently deleted (stronger than 404)
Spring Boot @Valid returns 400 by default — many teams override to 422 for validation errors

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: I distinguish 4xx codes carefully. 400 is for truly malformed requests — unparseable JSON or completely missing required fields. 404 is when the resource with that ID simply doesn't exist. 409 is for conflicts with current state — like trying to register an email that's already in use. 422 is for valid-looking requests that fail semantic validation — correct JSON, but age is minus 5. In Spring Boot, @Valid throws MethodArgumentNotValidException which maps to 400 by default, but many teams configure it to return 422 since validation is a semantic issue, not a syntax issue.

seo.metaTitle: 400 vs 404 vs 409 vs 422 HTTP Status Codes | Java Backend Interview

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: The 4xx range is all client error — but the specific code tells the client exactly what they did wrong.

beats.text: Choosing the right 4xx code helps API clients handle errors programmatically — retry, redirect the user to fix input, or show a conflict message. Using 400 for everything loses that precision.

items: 400 Bad Request: the request itself is malformed — unparseable JSON, completely missing required fields, wrong data type
404 Not Found: the resource with that ID simply doesn't exist
409 Conflict: the request conflicts with current server state — duplicate email, username taken, optimistic locking version mismatch
422 Unprocessable Entity: the request parses fine but fails semantic validation — age is -5, email format is wrong, a required future date is in the past

values: Fix the request format and resend
Resolve the conflict (use a different email, reload the resource)
Fix the input values and resend

beats.text: Think of it this way: 400 is a syntax problem, 422 is a value problem, 409 is a state problem, 404 is a missing resource. In Spring Boot, @Valid throws MethodArgumentNotValidException which maps to 400 by default — many teams override this to 422 for validation failures.

items: You're returning 400 for validation failures — 422 is more semantically correct; the JSON parsed fine, the values are wrong
You're returning 400 for a duplicate email conflict — that's 409; the request was valid, the state is the problem

speakable_v2.cap: 400 = malformed request. 404 = resource missing. 409 = state conflict. 422 = valid request, invalid values. Each tells the client a different thing to do next.

question: How do you implement consistent error responses in Spring Boot?
title: Spring Boot Error Response Design
direct_answer: Use @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods to catch exceptions globally and return structured error responses with appropriate status codes. Spring Boot's ProblemDetail (RFC 9457) provides a standard error response format.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Spring Boot knowledge for production-quality error handling
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Letting Spring return its default Whitelabel Error Page or inconsistent error formats
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention RFC 9457 Problem Details and mention not leaking stack traces in production

sections.title: Global Exception Handling in Spring Boot
sections.content: Without a global exception handler, Spring Boot either returns its Whitelabel Error Page (HTML) or inconsistent JSON. @ControllerAdvice acts as a global interceptor that catches exceptions from any controller and maps them to consistent error responses.

sections.title: Implementation Pattern
content: @ControllerAdvice class with @ExceptionHandler methods
Return ErrorResponse record: {timestamp, status, error, message, path}
@ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class) → 404
@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class) → 400/422 with field errors
@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) → 500 (catch-all, never expose stack trace)
Spring Boot 3: ProblemDetail (RFC 9457) is built in — use ResponseEntityExceptionHandler
Never include stack traces in production error responses

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: I use @ControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler to handle errors globally. I create a standard ErrorResponse structure with timestamp, status code, message, and path. Each exception type maps to a specific handler — ResourceNotFoundException returns 404, validation exceptions return 422 with field-level details, and a catch-all Exception handler returns 500. Critical rule: never include stack traces in production responses — log them server-side but return only a safe error message. In Spring Boot 3, ProblemDetail from RFC 9457 is built-in and provides a standard format that's becoming the industry norm.

seo.metaTitle: Spring Boot Error Handling @ControllerAdvice | Java Backend Interview
seo.metaDescription: Learn global error handling in Spring Boot with @ControllerAdvice and ProblemDetail. Fresher prep.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot 3.2 REST API for a todo app with GET, POST, PUT, DELETE endpoints
speakable_v2.hook: Without a global exception handler, Spring Boot returns HTML error pages or inconsistent JSON — @ControllerAdvice is how you take control.

beats.text: @ControllerAdvice is a Spring class that acts as a global interceptor for exceptions thrown by any controller. You write @ExceptionHandler methods inside it that catch specific exception types and return consistent, structured error responses.

Without it, every controller would need its own try-catch, and Spring would fall back to its Whitelabel Error Page (HTML) or expose a default JSON error map that leaks implementation details. @ControllerAdvice gives you a single place to handle all errors consistently.

items: @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class): returns 404 with a clean error body
@ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class): returns 400 or 422 with field-level validation errors
@ExceptionHandler(Exception.class): catch-all that returns 500 — never expose stack traces in production
Spring Boot 3 ProblemDetail (RFC 9457): built-in standard error format with type, title, status, detail, and instance fields

beats.text: Todo app: when GET /todos/999 throws TodoNotFoundException, the @ExceptionHandler maps it to 404 with {status: 404, message: Todo not found, timestamp: 2026-06-02T10:00:00}. When POST /todos with an invalid body triggers @Valid failure, the @ExceptionHandler for MethodArgumentNotValidException collects field errors and returns 422 with {errors: [{field: title, message: must not be blank}]}. In Spring Boot 3, you can extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler and return ProblemDetail objects for RFC-compliant error responses. production trap: the catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) must log the stack trace server-side but must never include it in the response body — stack traces reveal internal structure to attackers.

items: Including stack traces in error responses — log them, don't send them; they reveal internal details to attackers
Not having a catch-all handler — without one, unhandled exceptions return Spring's Whitelabel page or inconsistent format

speakable_v2.cap: @ControllerAdvice + @ExceptionHandler = one place for all error handling. Map exceptions to status codes, return a consistent body, never expose stack traces.
